ADHD Medications

stimulants · atomoxetine · alpha-2 agonistsStimulant or not, and what do you monitor?

Practice
  1. 9-year-old boy with ADHD; his parents agree to start a stimulant inattention and impulsivity at home and school for 2 years his uncle died suddenly while running at age 28 HR 88/min · BP 104/66 mm Hg · normal heart sounds → Electrocardiogram → sudden cardiac death in the family calls for an ECG before a stimulant, even with a normal exam
  2. 4-year-old boy brought by his mother for his behavior at home runs off in stores, climbs furniture, interrupts constantly same reports from his preschool teacher for 8 months no injuries; development otherwise normal → Parent training in behavior management → under age 6, behavioral therapy (parent training) comes first; medication is considered if it fails or the behavior puts anyone at risk
  3. 16-year-old boy with ADHD returns after his methylphenidate ran out early his mother found classmates paying him for pills grades slipping; symptoms clearly impair him HR 76/min · BP 118/72 mm Hg → Atomoxetine → a diverted stimulant calls for a nonstimulant: atomoxetine has no addiction risk
  4. 34-year-old woman with ADHD and depression asks to start an ADHD drug stopped phenelzine, taken for depression, 5 days ago takes no other medications HR 72/min · BP 116/74 mm Hg → Wait until 14 days after the last phenelzine dose → stimulants and atomoxetine are contraindicated within 14 days of stopping an MAOI (monoamine oxidase inhibitor)
  5. 11-year-old girl on atomoxetine for 3 months for ADHD 4 days of itching, dark urine and fatigue yellow sclerae; tender right upper quadrant ALT 640 U/L · AST 520 U/L · T 37.0 °C → Stop atomoxetine and do not restart it → jaundice or laboratory evidence of liver injury on atomoxetine: stop it and never restart
  6. 12-year-old boy with ADHD has a headache and feels jittery took guanfacine every day for a year; ran out 3 days ago no stimulant; no new drugs BP 148/96 mm Hg · HR 112/min · pupils normal → Rebound hypertension from stopping guanfacine → guanfacine stopped abruptly brings rebound hypertension and a fast pulse; it is tapered instead
  7. 15-year-old girl with ADHD, on amphetamine for 2 years 6 days of sleeping 2 hours a night without fatigue talks rapidly; plans to start three businesses urine drug screen negative · HR 90/min → Stop the amphetamine and treat the mania → a distinct episode with little need for sleep is mania, not ADHD; the stimulant is tapered or stopped and the mania treated first
Pairs with Tics and Tic Disorders covers ADHD with tics.
Eating Disorders covers lisdexamfetamine for binge eating.
Substance Intoxication and Withdrawal covers stimulant intoxication and misuse.
SNRIs, Atypical Antidepressants and MAOIs covers the MAOI washout.
Transferable rule

Before an ADHD drug, check the heart, the growth chart and the risk of misuse; misuse calls for atomoxetine, and an alpha-2 agonist is tapered, never stopped abruptly.
